title: 12 pre-registered crypto strategies, 0 survived costs + placebo tests. Where do retail traders actually find an edge?
author: worldrecchicken
selftext:
I've spent the last weeks building a strict research pipeline for BTC/ETH spot trading (EUR pairs). Everything has been tested on historical data and in paper trading, with no real money yet. My methodology is probably stricter than most hobby setups. The result: **nothing survives**. I'd like to hear from people who got further, or who hit the same wall.

**My setup (the rules I hold myself to)**

* Criteria are written down and committed to git **before** each test and never changed afterwards.
* Costs are always included: 0.25%/side in early tests, now 0.10%/side (taker), plus slippage.
* Strict walk-forward. The result has to hold per year and per market regime.
* Placebo test: 1,000 block-bootstrapped fake price series. A strategy only counts as "proven" at **p < 0.01**.
* Bar: beat buy-and-hold after costs **and** have a smaller max drawdown, with 99% intervals and a Bonferroni-style correction for the number of attempts.
* A held-out "vault" dataset (Bitstamp 2018–Mar 2019) that nobody has looked at. Each strategy gets exactly one shot at it.
* A hard cap of 13 attempts in total. If nothing works by then, my conclusion is "not feasible at these costs".
* No LLMs in the trading decision. They have seen the future in their training data.

**What I tested (all failed)**

|\#|Strategy|Result|
|:-|:-|:-|
||
|1–3|Time-series momentum, 24h/72h/168h lookback, vol-scaled, daily rebalance|Failed (168h closest: ETH p = 0.013)|
|4|Intraday momentum around the US open (14–15 UTC signal, hold until 21 UTC)|Failed|
|5–7|Online learning over these "experts" (Hedge, 1/N mix, Fixed Share)|Failed (Sharpe below buy-and-hold)|
|8|Momentum variant with a different volatility estimator|Failed|
|9|5-min breakout (close > 4h high)|≈ placebo, −0.55%/trade after costs|
|10|5-min dip-buy (1h drop > 2σ)|≈ placebo, −0.55%/trade|
|11|Panic-day buying|≈ placebo (p 0.47–0.48)|
|12|Slow trend filter on a broad coin basket|Sharpe 0.55 vs buy-and-hold 0.60. Smaller drawdown (77% vs 88%), but p = 0.57 and only 3/7 years positive|

Other findings:

* 0 of 240 flexible-exit variants were positive, and 0 of 270 "conditions" from a trade journal were positive. **The exit isn't the problem. The entry has no edge.**
* Paper trading confirmed this. A dip rule went 10/10 winners in one night, but that was one single recovery move, not 10 independent trades. The backtest over 7 years says it's placebo-level.
* After FOMC decisions crypto volatility roughly doubles in the following hour (BTC 0.66% → 1.25%), but the direction is unknown, so there's nothing tradeable.
* Lead-lag between exchanges: the lead I measured is ≤ 0.06%, far below the cost of a round trip.
* With \~0.2–0.5% friction per round trip, even a near-perfect predictor at horizons under 1 hour earns almost nothing.

**Where I'm stuck: my real questions**

1. **Source of edge.** For a retail trader without colocation or speed, what edge in crypto spot is *documented* to survive 0.1–0.2% costs? Is it structural (liquidation cascades, funding imbalances, forced selling, order book imbalance) rather than price patterns?
2. **Is my bar too strict, or the right one?** p < 0.01 against block-bootstrap placebos, plus beating buy-and-hold on Sharpe *and* drawdown. How do serious shops set this bar for single-asset strategies?
3. **Beating buy-and-hold in crypto.** BTC/ETH buy-and-hold has a huge drift. Should a timing strategy be benchmarked against risk-adjusted buy-and-hold, or against cash?
4. **Regime dependence.** Many strategies seem to work in one regime only. Is it legitimate to run a regime-switching approach, or is that overfitting in disguise?
5. **Paper vs live.** How far did your paper results drift from live (fills, slippage, latency)?
6. **Has anyone gotten past this point?** Not "my backtest is great", but sustained live profit after costs on BTC/ETH spot. What was the edge, and how long did it last?

**What's running now:** paper trading 24/7 on real exchange data, with 42 strategies in a "sandbox" that each have a pre-set required number of trades and a deadline. I'm also collecting order book, liquidation and lead-lag data for months before forming new hypotheses.

I'm happy to share the methodology. Honest stories about **what didn't work for you** are especially welcome. That's the rarest information online.

comments.author: Individual-Quote-958
comments.body: Your bar sounds right, not too harsh. Most retail "edges" that look great pre-cost are just measuring momentum or volatility clustering that fees and adverse selection eat. After costs, the things that sometimes survive for me are boring: tighter execution assumptions, fewer parameters, and ideas tied to a concrete market friction (funding, inventory, forced flows) instead of another indicator combo. Placebo and held-out dying is useful signal; it means the search process was honest. If nothing clears that bar, I would shrink the search space hard before adding more strategies. One well-specified hypothesis beat twelve clever ones every time I checked.

replies.author: worldrecchicken
replies.body:
This is the most useful answer so far. i'm already collecting liquidation and order book data, so "forced flows" fits what i have.

if you don't mind me asking which friction actually survived costs for you? and on spot only (no shorting), would you look at buying after a big liquidation wave, or is that already too crowded?

replies.author: Individual-Quote-958
replies.body: Honestly I don't have one I'd put real size behind yet, so take this as where I'd look, not a result. Spot only, I'd test buying after the liquidation wave is done rather than during it, like once open interest stops dropping and funding resets, then hold for a fixed window. Compare it against random entries with the same hold time, since a lot of these just catch the bounce any dip buy gets.
